[strategy/guidance/governance/implementation/GUID-GOV-IMPL-003-ai-agent-spec-authoring-guidance.md#purpose-statement]

### Purpose Statement

This guidance teaches engineers and analysts how to write a well-formed agent task spec — the structured issue body that the AI agent dispatch pipeline reads, validates, and executes. It covers when to use an agent task (and when not to), how to write each of the four required sections, how to calibrate acceptance criteria granularity, how to choose the right routing label, and what the authoring workflow looks like from first draft to pipeline trigger.
page_texts.5:
[strategy/guidance/governance/implementation/GUID-GOV-IMPL-003-ai-agent-spec-authoring-guidance.md#business-value]

### Business Value

- **Higher first-run success rate** — a well-formed spec passes validation and produces useful agent output on the first attempt; a poorly-formed spec cycles through multiple failed runs
- **Predictable agent scope** — clear acceptance criteria and constraints keep the agent focused; vague specs produce over-broad or off-target output
- **Audit trail quality** — every spec is a traceable requirement; well-written specs make the audit trail meaningful, not just present

[strategy/guidance/governance/implementation/GUID-GOV-IMPL-003-ai-agent-spec-authoring-guidance.md#business-drivers]

#### Business Drivers

The spec is the single document that drives everything downstream: it is validated by the pipeline, executed by the agent, reviewed by the human, and preserved as the audit record linking a deployment back to its business requirement. The quality of the spec determines the quality of the output. STD-GOV-AI-001 defines what the spec MUST contain; this guidance explains HOW to write each section well — the craft behind the standard.

[strategy/guidance/governance/implementation/GUID-GOV-IMPL-003-ai-agent-spec-authoring-guidance.md#step-0-decompose-from-user-story-to-agent-specs]

### Step 0: Decompose from User Story to Agent Specs

Before writing any spec, determine how many GitHub Issues the upstream ADO User Story requires. A User Story is a unit of business value that a human plans and estimates; a GitHub Issue spec is a unit of autonomous agent execution. These are not the same granularity.
page_texts.15:
[strategy/guidance/governance/implementation/GUID-GOV-IMPL-003-ai-agent-spec-authoring-guidance.md#the-mapping-rule]

#### The mapping rule

**One ADO User Story → one or more GitHub Issues.** The relationship is always one-to-many (or one-to-one for trivially small stories). A single Issue per story is correct only when the entire story scope is a single atomic deliverable that one agent can complete in one pipeline run.
page_texts.16:
[strategy/guidance/governance/implementation/GUID-GOV-IMPL-003-ai-agent-spec-authoring-guidance.md#why-stories-must-be-decomposed]

#### Why stories must be decomposed

| Constraint | Implication |
|---|---||
| One pipeline run produces one PR | A PR covering 10 files across 3 domains is unreviable; keep each PR focused |
| Agent context window is bounded | A spec covering a full feature's implementation, docs, and tests exceeds what the agent can hold coherently |
| Each routing label targets a different agent config | `agent:implementation` and `agent:documentation` work cannot share a spec — they route to different agents |
| SOD requires a second-party label application (ADR-GOV-010) | A reviewer cannot meaningfully apply `agent-task` to a spec that is too large to evaluate |
page_texts.17:
[strategy/guidance/governance/implementation/GUID-GOV-IMPL-003-ai-agent-spec-authoring-guidance.md#decomposition-signals]

#### Decomposition signals

Use these signals to identify seam points within a User Story:

**1. Acceptance criteria scenarios → Issues (primary signal)**
Each Given/When/Then scenario in the User Story acceptance criteria describes an independently verifiable outcome. If the scenarios can be validated independently, each is a candidate for its own Issue.

**2. Routing label boundaries (hard boundary)**
If the story spans multiple agent types (`agent:implementation`, `agent:documentation`, `agent:testing`, `agent:infrastructure`), those portions MUST be separate Issues. A single spec receives exactly one routing label.

**3. File count heuristic**
If executing the story would touch more than 5 files, split it. Each Issue should produce a PR of 1–5 files.

**4. Artifact type cohesion (for documentation stories)**
For EA documentation work, the natural seam is artifact type: standards together, ADRs together, guidance documents together, patterns together. Authoring conventions and cross-references within each type are coherent; mixing types in a single agent session produces inconsistent output.
page_texts.18:
[strategy/guidance/governance/implementation/GUID-GOV-IMPL-003-ai-agent-spec-authoring-guidance.md#decomposition-process]

#### Decomposition process

```
1. Read the User Story acceptance criteria
   └─ List each scenario

2. Group scenarios by routing label
   ├─ All implementation work → agent:implementation Issues
   ├─ All documentation work → agent:documentation Issues
   ├─ All test work          → agent:testing Issues
   └─ All IaC work           → agent:infrastructure Issues

3. Within each label group, apply the file count heuristic
   └─ If a group would produce > 5 files, split into multiple Issues

4. For each resulting Issue:
   ├─ Write one Goal sentence (Step 2 below)
   ├─ Map the relevant AC scenarios from the User Story
   └─ Record the ADO work item ID in the Enterprise Work Item section

5. Reference the ADO User Story in every Issue
   └─ Include "AB#<story-id>" in the Enterprise Work Item section
```
page_texts.19:
[strategy/guidance/governance/implementation/GUID-GOV-IMPL-003-ai-agent-spec-authoring-guidance.md#example-decomposition]

#### Example decomposition

ADO User Story AB#4821 (5 story points): *"Add rate limiting to the Claims API so that downstream services are protected from burst traffic."*

Acceptance criteria scenarios:
1. `POST /claims` returns HTTP 429 with `Retry-After` header when limit exceeded
2. Limit is configurable per environment via environment variable
3. Unit tests cover the four rate-limit boundary scenarios
4. OpenAPI spec documents the 429 response on all affected endpoints

Decomposition — spans three routing labels, so three Issues, with a required execution order:

| Issue | Scope | Files | Label | Order |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Issue 1 | Add rate-limiting middleware to `src/api/claims/middleware/`; wire into request pipeline | 3 | `agent:implementation` | 1st |
| Issue 2 | Write unit tests for rate-limit boundary cases in `tests/unit/claims/` | 2 | `agent:testing` | 2nd — prerequisite: Issue 1 merged |
| Issue 3 | Update `docs/api/claims-api.yaml` (OpenAPI) to document 429 responses on affected endpoints | 1 | `agent:documentation` | Parallel with Issue 2 |

Each Issue references `AB#4821` in its Enterprise Work Item section. Issues 1 and 3 can be triggered in parallel if the OpenAPI spec already contains the endpoint definitions. Issue 2 must wait for Issue 1 to merge — the middleware must exist before tests can be written against it.
page_texts.20:
[strategy/guidance/governance/implementation/GUID-GOV-IMPL-003-ai-agent-spec-authoring-guidance.md#handling-prerequisites-between-issues]

#### Handling prerequisites between Issues

When one Issue depends on another being merged before the agent can succeed (e.g., `agent:testing` tests code that `agent:implementation` must create first), the pipeline has no native enforcement mechanism. Use the following approach:

**Step 1: Express the dependency in the Constraints section**

Add a prerequisite line to the dependent spec's `## Constraints` section. The agent reads this and will surface a failure if the referenced file or PR is not yet present in the repository:

```markdown
## Constraints
- Prerequisite: Issue #<N> must be merged before this task begins; the file `<path>` it creates is required
- ...
```

**Step 2: Use the SOD reviewer as the enforcement gate**

The SOD control (ADR-GOV-010) already requires a second party to apply `agent-task`. This human gate is the correct enforcement point for ordering. The reviewer's checklist (GUID-GOV-IMPL-004) must include:

> *If the spec declares a prerequisite, verify the prerequisite PR is merged before applying `agent-task`.*

Do not apply `agent-task` to a blocked Issue until its prerequisite is closed.

**Step 3: Design for parallelism where possible**

Ordering is only required when outputs are inputs. Review the decomposition and ask: *does this Issue read a file that another Issue writes?* If not, the Issues are independent and can be triggered in any order or concurrently. For documentation and infrastructure work, most Issues within the same story are parallel-safe. For implementation → testing sequences, ordering is always required.

**Summary of mechanisms**

| Scenario | Mechanism | Enforced by |
|---|---|---|
| Agent must not run until prerequisite is merged | `Prerequisite:` line in `## Constraints` | Agent (surfaces missing file); SOD reviewer (holds label) |
| Prevent premature pipeline trigger | Do not apply `agent-task` until prerequisite is closed | SOD reviewer |
| No ordering required | Design for parallelism — independent file sets | Architecture (decomposition step) |

[strategy/guidance/governance/implementation/GUID-GOV-IMPL-003-ai-agent-spec-authoring-guidance.md#step-1-should-this-task-be-an-agent-task]

### Step 1: Should This Task Be an Agent Task?

Before writing a spec, decide whether the task is appropriate for autonomous agent execution. Use this decision tree:

```
Is the task's scope clearly bounded by a single, atomic deliverable?
│
├─ NO ──► Break the work into smaller atomic tasks first.
│          Each agent task must be completable in a single pipeline run.
│          (Complex features decompose into: implement → document → test — three specs)
│
└─ YES
   │
   Can the "done" state be verified by automated checks (tests, lint, build)?
   │
   ├─ NO ──► Consider a human task.
   │          Agents cannot verify subjective quality. If "done" requires
   │          human aesthetic judgment (e.g., "improve the UX"), it is not
   │          agent-appropriate without additional automated acceptance checks.
   │
   └─ YES
      │
      Is the task free from decision-making that requires business context
      not expressible in the spec? (i.e., the agent can proceed without
      asking clarifying questions)
      │
      ├─ NO ──► Resolve the ambiguity first.
      │          Add the decision outcome to the Constraints section,
      │          then re-evaluate.
      │
      └─ YES
         │
         Does the task involve reading or writing PHI / PII?
         │
         ├─ YES ──► NOT agent-appropriate.
         │           Agent task specs are stored in the issue tracker, which
         │           must not contain PHI. If the feature touches PHI-adjacent
         │           code, the spec must be scoped to the structural/technical
         │           aspect only (e.g., "Add audit logging to the data access
         │           layer") — never to the data content.
         │
         └─ NO ──► ✅ Proceed to write the spec.
```
page_texts.22:
[strategy/guidance/governance/implementation/GUID-GOV-IMPL-003-ai-agent-spec-authoring-guidance.md#task-types-that-are-consistently-agent-appropriate]

#### Task types that are consistently agent-appropriate

| Task Type | Example Goal |
|---|---|
| Adding a feature following an existing pattern | "Add a `/health` endpoint to the patient-service API following the pattern in `/users/health`." |
| Generating documentation from code | "Generate OpenAPI 3.1 documentation for all endpoints in `src/api/claims/`." |
| Adding tests for existing code | "Write unit tests for `ClaimsProcessor.calculate()` targeting 90% branch coverage." |
| Implementing a standard-defined pattern | "Add structured JSON logging to all Lambda functions in `src/functions/` per the logging standard." |
| Infrastructure scaffolding from a template | "Create a Terraform module for an S3 bucket with server-side encryption following `iac/modules/s3-encrypted/`." |
| Applying a consistent change across files | "Update all Python files in `src/` to replace `print()` statements with structured logger calls." |
page_texts.23:
[strategy/guidance/governance/implementation/GUID-GOV-IMPL-003-ai-agent-spec-authoring-guidance.md#task-types-that-are-not-agent-appropriate-without-further-decomposition]

#### Task types that are NOT agent-appropriate without further decomposition

| Task Type | Why Not | Decomposition Approach |
|---|---|---|
| "Build the claims processing service" | Too large; not atomic | Decompose into 10+ individual tasks by endpoint/component |
| "Improve API performance" | No objective done state | Define specific: "Add Redis caching to `ClaimsService.getClaim()` with 5-minute TTL" |
| "Review and clean up the codebase" | No bounded scope | Not agent-appropriate; use optimizer/reviewer skills |
| "Fix the bug in the payment module" | Ambiguous; requires diagnosis | Diagnose first (human task), then write a spec for the specific fix |
| "Design the new data model" | Architecture decision, not implementation | Architecture work first (human/architect); agent implements once design is complete |

page_texts.24:
[strategy/guidance/governance/implementation/GUID-GOV-IMPL-003-ai-agent-spec-authoring-guidance.md#step-2-write-the-goal-section]

### Step 2: Write the Goal Section

The Goal section is a single sentence that defines the complete, bounded scope of the agent task.
page_texts.25:
[strategy/guidance/governance/implementation/GUID-GOV-IMPL-003-ai-agent-spec-authoring-guidance.md#rules]

#### Rules

1. **One sentence.** If you need a second sentence, the task is too large or under-constrained — split it or add the clarification to Constraints.
2. **Start with an action verb.** The verb signals what the agent must DO: Add, Generate, Implement, Update, Remove, Create, Migrate, Refactor.
3. **Name the specific target.** Don't say "the service" — say "`patient-service`". Don't say "the logging" — say "structured JSON logging in `src/api/`".
4. **Include the scope boundary.** If the task applies to a subset of the codebase, name it: "in all Lambda functions", "to the `/claims` endpoints only", "for `ClaimsProcessor` and `PaymentProcessor`".
page_texts.26:
[strategy/guidance/governance/implementation/GUID-GOV-IMPL-003-ai-agent-spec-authoring-guidance.md#goal-sentence-patterns-by-agent-type]

#### Goal sentence patterns by agent type

| Agent Type | Pattern | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `agent:implementation` | Add/Implement/Create `<feature>` to/in `<target>` | "Add rate-limiting middleware (100 req/min per IP) to the API gateway." |
| `agent:implementation` | Update `<target>` to `<change>` | "Update all `fetch()` calls in `src/api/` to use the shared `httpClient` wrapper." |
| `agent:documentation` | Generate `<doc type>` for `<target>` | "Generate OpenAPI 3.1 documentation for all endpoints in `src/api/claims/`." |
| `agent:documentation` | Document `<target>` in `<format/location>` | "Document the `ClaimsProcessor` class methods with Google-style docstrings." |
| `agent:testing` | Write `<test type>` tests for `<target>` targeting `<coverage>` | "Write unit tests for `ClaimsProcessor.calculate()` targeting 90% branch coverage." |
| `agent:testing` | Add integration tests for `<scenario>` in `<target>` | "Add integration tests for the claims submission happy path in `tests/integration/`." |
| `agent:infrastructure` | Create a Terraform module for `<resource>` following `<template>` | "Create a Terraform module for an S3 bucket with server-side encryption following `iac/modules/s3-encrypted/`." |
| `agent:infrastructure` | Add `<resource/config>` to `<target environment/file>` | "Add CloudWatch log retention (90 days) to all Lambda functions in `iac/formations/claims-service/`." |
page_texts.27:
[strategy/guidance/governance/implementation/GUID-GOV-IMPL-003-ai-agent-spec-authoring-guidance.md#common-goal-writing-mistakes]

#### Common Goal writing mistakes

| Mistake | Problem | Correction |
|---|---|---|
| "Fix the API" | No scope, no action | "Add input validation for null values to the `POST /claims` endpoint." |
| "Improve logging across the system" | No bounded target | "Add structured JSON logging to `src/api/claims/` replacing all `console.log()` calls." |
| "Add tests and documentation" | Two tasks combined | Split into two issues: one `agent:testing`, one `agent:documentation` |
| "Implement the new feature per the design doc" | Requires reading external document not in context | Include the relevant design constraints inline in the Constraints section |
| "Update the code to be better" | No objective success criterion | Not agent-appropriate; define specific improvement |

page_texts.28:
[strategy/guidance/governance/implementation/GUID-GOV-IMPL-003-ai-agent-spec-authoring-guidance.md#step-3-write-the-acceptance-criteria-section]

### Step 3: Write the Acceptance Criteria Section

Acceptance criteria define the agent's "done" state in terms that automated checks can verify.
page_texts.29:
[strategy/guidance/governance/implementation/GUID-GOV-IMPL-003-ai-agent-spec-authoring-guidance.md#rules]

#### Rules

1. **Minimum 2 items.** A single criterion doesn't bound the scope adequately.
2. **Checkable format.** Use `- [ ]` GitHub Flavored Markdown checkboxes. This is required by the pipeline validator and makes the reviewer's job clear.
3. **At least one technical/verifiable criterion.** "Works correctly" is not checkable. "All existing tests pass" is. "Unit test coverage for `ClaimsProcessor.calculate()` ≥ 90%" is.
4. **Write from the reviewer's perspective.** Each criterion should complete: "I can verify this is done by..."
page_texts.30:
[strategy/guidance/governance/implementation/GUID-GOV-IMPL-003-ai-agent-spec-authoring-guidance.md#granularity-calibration]

#### Granularity calibration

A common question is how detailed criteria should be. The answer depends on the agent's routing type:

| Agent Type | Granularity Level | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| `agent:implementation` | Outcome-level + one structural | Agent has discretion on implementation approach; constrain the outcome, not the method |
| `agent:documentation` | Format + completeness | Agent generates text; define what must be present (sections, examples, return types) |
| `agent:testing` | Coverage metric + test pattern | Agent writes tests; define the coverage target and which test patterns to follow |
| `agent:infrastructure` | Resource properties + idempotency | Agent generates IaC; define key resource properties and that `terraform plan` produces no errors |
page_texts.31:
[strategy/guidance/governance/implementation/GUID-GOV-IMPL-003-ai-agent-spec-authoring-guidance.md#acceptance-criteria-patterns]

#### Acceptance criteria patterns

```markdown
# Implementation — outcome-level
- [ ] The `POST /claims` endpoint returns HTTP 422 with a structured error body when the `memberId` field is null
- [ ] All existing tests continue to pass (`npm test` exits 0)
- [ ] No new dependencies are introduced without a comment linking to the dependency decision

# Documentation — format + completeness
- [ ] Every public method in `ClaimsProcessor` has a Google-style docstring with Args, Returns, and Raises sections
- [ ] The generated docstrings are syntactically valid Python (`python -m py_compile` exits 0)
- [ ] At least one usage example is included for `ClaimsProcessor.calculate()`

# Testing — coverage + pattern
- [ ] Unit test coverage for `ClaimsProcessor.calculate()` is ≥ 90% branch coverage (measured by `pytest --cov`)
- [ ] Each test follows the `test_<method>_<condition>_<expected>` naming convention
- [ ] No tests use hardcoded test data that resembles real member or claim identifiers

# Infrastructure — resource properties + idempotency
- [ ] The Terraform module provisions an S3 bucket with `server_side_encryption_configuration` using `AES256`
- [ ] `terraform plan` on the module with default variables produces 0 errors and 0 destructive changes
- [ ] The module exposes `bucket_name` and `bucket_arn` as outputs
```
page_texts.32:
[strategy/guidance/governance/implementation/GUID-GOV-IMPL-003-ai-agent-spec-authoring-guidance.md#anti-patterns-to-avoid]

#### Anti-patterns to avoid

| Anti-pattern | Why it fails | Replacement |
|---|---|---|
| `- [ ] The implementation looks clean` | Subjective; not checkable | `- [ ] All new functions are ≤30 lines (measured by pylint)` |
| `- [ ] Works as expected` | No definition of expected | Define the specific expected behavior |
| `- [ ] The agent did a good job` | Not meaningful after the fact | Remove; replace with testable criteria |
| `- [ ] No bugs` | Not verifiable before deployment | `- [ ] All unit tests pass; no new lint errors` |
| 10+ criteria for a small task | Over-specified; constrains implementation unnecessarily | Target 2–5 criteria; move extra constraints to the Constraints section |

---
page_texts.33:
[strategy/guidance/governance/implementation/GUID-GOV-IMPL-003-ai-agent-spec-authoring-guidance.md#step-4-write-the-constraints-section]

### Step 4: Write the Constraints Section

Constraints are the guardrails the agent MUST respect — standards to follow, patterns to match, files not to touch, and boundaries not to cross.
page_texts.34:
[strategy/guidance/governance/implementation/GUID-GOV-IMPL-003-ai-agent-spec-authoring-guidance.md#rules]

#### Rules

1. **Minimum 2 constraints.** One is rarely sufficient to prevent unwanted behavior.
2. **Reference explicitly.** Don't say "follow our coding standards" — say "follow `standards/application/api-standards.md § 4.2` for response envelope format".
3. **Name files the agent should follow as a pattern.** "Match the pattern in `src/api/users/` when implementing `src/api/claims/`" is far more useful than a general style constraint.
4. **Add scope limits.** "Only modify files in `src/api/claims/`" tells the agent not to touch adjacent modules.
5. **Include what NOT to do.** Negative constraints are often the most important: "Do not introduce new npm packages", "Do not modify database migration files", "Do not change the public API contract".
page_texts.35:
[strategy/guidance/governance/implementation/GUID-GOV-IMPL-003-ai-agent-spec-authoring-guidance.md#constraint-categories-and-patterns]

#### Constraint categories and patterns

```markdown
## Constraints

# Standards reference
- Follow `standards/application/api-standards.md § 4.2` for all response envelopes
- Follow `standards/technology/python/` for code style (black, ruff, type annotations)

# Pattern matching
- Match the implementation pattern in `src/api/users/health.py` when adding the new endpoint
- Use the existing `httpClient` wrapper in `src/utils/http.py` — do not use `fetch()` directly

# Scope limits
- Only modify files in `src/api/claims/` and `tests/unit/claims/`
- Do not modify `src/models/` — schema changes are out of scope

# Prohibitions
- Do not introduce new npm packages not already in `package.json`
- Do not change the public method signatures of `ClaimsProcessor` — callers depend on them
- Do not add TODO or FIXME comments — all changes must be complete

# Data safety (always include for any task touching data handling)
- Do not use real member IDs, claim IDs, or any production data in test fixtures
- Use the synthetic data generator in `tests/fixtures/generate.py`
```
page_texts.36:
[strategy/guidance/governance/implementation/GUID-GOV-IMPL-003-ai-agent-spec-authoring-guidance.md#when-not-to-over-constrain]

#### When not to over-constrain

Too many constraints reduce the agent's ability to make sensible implementation choices and can make the spec impossible to satisfy. Signs of over-constraining:

- More than 8–10 constraints for a single task
- Constraints that specify HOW to implement (algorithm choice, variable names) rather than WHAT constraints apply
- Conflicting constraints (e.g., "follow the users module pattern" AND "do not use the httpClient wrapper that the users module uses")

If you find yourself writing very detailed implementation instructions in the Constraints section, consider whether this is better handled by adding a reference to an existing well-documented pattern, or whether the task requires human implementation because the approach requires judgment.

---

[strategy/guidance/governance/implementation/GUID-GOV-IMPL-003-ai-agent-spec-authoring-guidance.md#step-5-write-the-enterprise-work-item-section]

### Step 5: Write the Enterprise Work Item Section

The Enterprise Work Item section contains the single cross-reference linking this spec to the business requirement in your enterprise work management system.
page_texts.38:
[strategy/guidance/governance/implementation/GUID-GOV-IMPL-003-ai-agent-spec-authoring-guidance.md#format-by-platform]

#### Format by platform

| Your Platform | Format | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Azure DevOps (internal link) | `WI#<numeric-id>` | `WI#4821` |
| Azure DevOps via GitHub link | `AB#<numeric-id>` | `AB#4821` |
| Jira | `<PROJECT>-<numeric-id>` | `PLAT-1234` |
| ServiceNow (change) | `CHG<numeric-id>` | `CHG0012345` |
| ServiceNow (incident) | `INC<numeric-id>` | `INC0012345` |

If you don't know your team's format, check with your Engineering Lead or look at recent PRs from the pipeline — the traceability block will show the format in use.
page_texts.39:
[strategy/guidance/governance/implementation/GUID-GOV-IMPL-003-ai-agent-spec-authoring-guidance.md#finding-your-work-item-id]

#### Finding your work item ID

The work item is the sprint task or user story that this agent task implements. If no work item exists yet, create it in the enterprise system first. The pipeline will not execute without a valid cross-reference — this is by design. Every agent execution must trace to a business requirement.

**If your task is not tracked in the enterprise system at all**, that is a process gap. Discuss with your Engineering Lead. Do not invent or fabricate a work item ID.

page_texts.40:
[strategy/guidance/governance/implementation/GUID-GOV-IMPL-003-ai-agent-spec-authoring-guidance.md#step-6-choose-the-routing-label]

### Step 6: Choose the Routing Label

Apply exactly one routing label before requesting peer review:

| Label | Use when the task produces... |
|---|---|
| `agent:implementation` | Working code (functions, classes, endpoints, modules) |
| `agent:documentation` | Documentation artifacts (docstrings, READMEs, API docs, comments) |
| `agent:testing` | Test files (unit tests, integration tests, test fixtures) |
| `agent:infrastructure` | Infrastructure as code (Terraform, Terragrunt, CloudFormation) |

**When the task spans multiple types:** Create separate issues. A task that requires "implement the endpoint AND write tests for it" becomes two issues: one `agent:implementation` and one `agent:testing`. The implementation PR must be merged first; the testing spec should reference the implementation PR number in its Constraints section.

[strategy/guidance/governance/implementation/GUID-GOV-IMPL-003-ai-agent-spec-authoring-guidance.md#the-authoring-workflow]

### The Authoring Workflow

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ 1. ASSESS — Apply the decision tree. Confirm it's agent-ready.  │
└────────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────────────┘
                             │
┌────────────────────────────▼────────────────────────────────────┐
│ 2. DRAFT — Write all four sections using the issue template.    │
│    Apply routing label. Do NOT apply agent-task yet.            │
└────────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────────────┘
                             │
┌────────────────────────────▼────────────────────────────────────┐
│ 3. SELF-REVIEW — Check against the quick-validation checklist.  │
└────────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────────────┘
                             │
┌────────────────────────────▼────────────────────────────────────┐
│ 4. PEER REVIEW — Assign to a reviewer (or request in sprint     │
│    planning). Reviewer checks STD-GOV-AI-001 compliance.        │
└────────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────────────┘
                             │
               ┌─────────────┴──────────────┐
               │ Changes needed?            │ Approved?
               ▼                            ▼
        Author revises             Reviewer applies agent-task
        → back to step 3           (this triggers the pipeline)
```

**Key principle:** The author NEVER applies `agent-task` themselves. The peer reviewer applies it as the approval signal that the spec is ready. This is equivalent to the "second set of eyes" control on production deployments.

[strategy/guidance/governance/implementation/GUID-GOV-IMPL-003-ai-agent-spec-authoring-guidance.md#self-review-checklist]

### Self-Review Checklist

Before requesting peer review, confirm each item:

**Goal:**
- [ ] Exactly one sentence
- [ ] Starts with an action verb
- [ ] Names the specific target (file, module, endpoint, resource)
- [ ] Includes a scope boundary

**Acceptance Criteria:**
- [ ] ≥2 items, each as `- [ ]` checkbox
- [ ] Each criterion is objectively verifiable (automated check or clear pass/fail)
- [ ] At least one criterion that an automated test or tool can validate
- [ ] No criteria that require subjective judgment

**Constraints:**
- [ ] ≥2 constraints
- [ ] Each references a specific standard, file, or pattern by path
- [ ] Includes at least one scope-limiting constraint ("only modify files in...")
- [ ] Includes at least one prohibition if there are common adjacent mistakes

**Enterprise Work Item:**
- [ ] Contains exactly one cross-reference in the correct format for your platform
- [ ] The work item exists and is active in the enterprise system

**Routing Label:**
- [ ] Exactly one routing label applied

page_texts.46:
[strategy/guidance/governance/implementation/GUID-GOV-IMPL-003-ai-agent-spec-authoring-guidance.md#when-the-pipeline-rejects-your-spec]

### When the Pipeline Rejects Your Spec

If the pipeline removes `agent-task` and posts a corrective comment, read the comment carefully — it names the specific validation that failed.

| Corrective message | What to fix |
|---|---|
| "Missing sections: Acceptance Criteria" | Add the missing section using `## Acceptance Criteria` as the exact header |
| "Fewer than 2 acceptance criteria checkboxes" | Add more `- [ ]` items; make sure they use GFM checkbox syntax |
| "Enterprise Work Item section does not contain a valid cross-reference" | Check your platform format (WI#, AB#, PROJ-123); update the section |
| "No routing label found" | Apply exactly one of the routing labels before re-applying `agent-task` |
| "Multiple routing labels found" | Remove all but one routing label |
| Security/PHI message | Review the issue body for content that shouldn't be there; contact your security team if the message appears to be a false positive |

After fixing the spec, re-apply `agent-task` to re-trigger the pipeline. You do NOT need to create a new issue.
page_texts.47:
[strategy/guidance/governance/implementation/GUID-GOV-IMPL-003-ai-agent-spec-authoring-guidance.md#when-the-agents-output-doesnt-match-your-intent]

### When the Agent's Output Doesn't Match Your Intent

If the agent produces a PR that doesn't address the goal correctly, the problem is almost always in the spec. Common causes:

| Symptom | Likely cause in spec | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Agent implemented something adjacent but not quite right | Goal scope too broad or ambiguous | Tighten the goal — name the exact function/file/endpoint |
| Agent modified files it shouldn't have | Missing scope-limit constraint | Add: "Only modify files in `<specific directory>`" |
| Agent used a different pattern than expected | Pattern reference missing from Constraints | Add: "Match the pattern in `<reference file>`" |
| Agent added a dependency you didn't want | Missing prohibition | Add: "Do not introduce new packages not already in `<dependency file>`" |
| Agent output is technically correct but misses the business intent | Acceptance criteria are too low-level | Raise one criterion to the behavior/outcome level |

Close the agent PR, update the spec, remove `agent:blocked` if present, and re-apply `agent-task`.

[strategy/guidance/governance/implementation/GUID-GOV-IMPL-003-ai-agent-spec-authoring-guidance.md#full-example-implementation-spec]

### Full Example: Implementation Spec

**Scenario:** Add rate limiting to an existing API gateway.

```markdown
## Goal

Add rate-limiting middleware (100 requests per minute per client IP) to the `api-gateway` service at `src/middleware/`.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] Requests exceeding the rate limit receive HTTP 429 with a `Retry-After` header indicating seconds until the limit resets
- [ ] The rate limit configuration (limit, window, storage backend) is read from environment variables, not hardcoded
- [ ] All existing middleware tests in `tests/unit/middleware/` continue to pass
- [ ] A unit test for the rate limiter covers: request within limit (200 expected), request at limit boundary (200), first request over limit (429)

## Constraints

- Follow `standards/application/api-standards.md § 4.2` for the HTTP 429 response envelope format
- Use the Redis client already configured in `src/utils/redis-client.ts` as the rate limit storage backend — do not introduce a new Redis client
- Match the middleware registration pattern in `src/middleware/auth.ts`
- Only modify files in `src/middleware/` and `tests/unit/middleware/`
- Do not modify `src/routes/` — middleware registration in the router is already correct
- Do not introduce new npm packages

## Enterprise Work Item

WI#4821
```

**Routing label:** `agent:implementation`
page_texts.50:
[strategy/guidance/governance/implementation/GUID-GOV-IMPL-003-ai-agent-spec-authoring-guidance.md#full-example-testing-spec]

### Full Example: Testing Spec

**Scenario:** Add tests for a recently merged implementation.

```markdown
## Goal

Write unit tests for `ClaimsProcessor.calculate()` in `src/processors/claims-processor.ts` targeting 90% branch coverage.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] Branch coverage for `ClaimsProcessor.calculate()` reaches ≥ 90% when running `npm run test:coverage`
- [ ] Each test follows the `describe('ClaimsProcessor') > describe('calculate') > it('should <behavior> when <condition>')` naming pattern
- [ ] Tests cover at minimum: valid claim calculation, null input handling, negative amount rejection, and maximum claim amount boundary
- [ ] No test uses hardcoded claim IDs, member IDs, or values that resemble production data

## Constraints

- Only create or modify files in `tests/unit/processors/`
- Use the test factory in `tests/factories/claims-factory.ts` for test data — do not create inline objects directly in tests
- Do not modify `src/processors/claims-processor.ts` — if a bug is discovered during test authoring, note it in a comment referencing the file and line; fixing it is out of scope
- Follow the testing standard at `standards/technology/testing/unit-test-standard.md`

## Enterprise Work Item

AB#4822
```

**Routing label:** `agent:testing`

## Governance and Compliance

- **STD-GOV-AI-001** governs what MUST be in every spec; this guidance explains how to write each section well
- The peer reviewer who applies `agent-task` is asserting STD-GOV-AI-001 compliance — they are accountable for that assertion
- Specs are preserved as part of the audit trail; retroactive modification of a spec after agent execution is prohibited
